analysis.one_liner: Eases proof standards for coal miners' black lung claims and shifts all benefit payments onto an industry-financed trust fund.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House subcommittee and died at the end of the 103rd Congress without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it much easier for coal miners to win black lung (pneumoconiosis) benefits: a single qualifying x-ray, breathing test, blood-gas test, or doctor's opinion would trigger a presumption of total disability, and 10 years of mine work would create a presumption the disease came from mining. It would require all benefits awarded under these easier standards to be paid out of the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which is financed by the coal industry, so coal operators could no longer be sued as defendants in these cases. It also would have let previously denied miners refile their claims, protected widows' benefits after remarriage regardless of marriage length, and barred the government from clawing back benefits paid before a final denial.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners disabled by black lung disease and their survivors. The bill would have created automatic presumptions of disability and work-causation that claimants no longer had to prove by a preponderance of the evidence, reopened denied claims for fresh review, guaranteed survivor benefits when a miner had 25 years of mine work, was already receiving benefits, or died of the disease, and ended the practice of demanding repayment when a claimant was later found ineligible.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal miners with black lung and their widows

how_it_helps.text: A single qualifying x-ray, biopsy, autopsy, set of ventilatory studies, set of blood-gas studies, or a physician's documented opinion would create a presumption of total disability from black lung, and claimants would not have to prove anything by a preponderance of the evidence [S2][S3].

A miner with 10 or more years in the mines would enjoy a rebuttable presumption that the disease arose from coal mine employment, provable with co-worker affidavits if Social Security records were incomplete [S3].
All benefits determined under the new standards would be paid from the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, eliminating coal operators as defendants with legal counsel in these cases [S2].

Claimants whose claims had been denied could file again without showing any change in circumstances, for fresh consideration on the merits, and the Secretary of Labor could not appeal adverse decisions or reopen awarded claims except on reasonable evidence of fraud [S2][S3].
Widows would keep benefits after remarrying and qualify regardless of how long they had been married to the miner, and benefits paid before a final denial would never have to be repaid [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal operators. The Black Lung Disability Trust Fund is financed by the coal industry, so paying every benefit from the fund shifts the full cost of easier awards onto coal companies through the excise tax that supports the fund [S2]. Coal companies would also lose their role as parties defending against claims with their own legal counsel [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal operators, through the industry-financed trust fund

drawbacks.text: The bill let a single positive x-ray, a single set of blood-gas studies, or one physician's opinion trigger a presumption of total disability that a physician's contrary opinion could not rebut when the qualifying test was invoked, which would award benefits in some cases where the diagnosis or work-causation was genuinely uncertain [S3].

Requiring every benefit to be paid from the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund would raise the excise-tax cost borne by the coal industry, a cost that can flow into coal prices, and would deepen claims on a fund that historically has needed infusions beyond industry taxes to stay solvent.

Claimants would have been able to refile denied claims indefinitely with no showing of a material change in circumstances, and benefits already paid could never be clawed back even after a final finding of ineligibility, raising cost and integrity concerns [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: miners and widows who could not meet demanding proof standards for a disease caused by years underground would get benefits without ruinous litigation. The main cost falls on the coal industry, whose operations produce the disease, though looser presumptions and no-repayment rules would also let some genuinely uncertain claims through and put pressure on the trust fund's finances. The bill gave opposing parties (the government as payer) less ability to contest awards, which helps claimants but weakens error-correction.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to its Labor Standards subcommittee on February 19, 1993, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended, so it never reached the floor [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Nick Rahall of West Virginia introduced the Black Lung Benefits Act Amendments of 1993 on February 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced, and on February 19, 1993 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, Occupational Health and Safety [S5].
No committee markup, hearing vote, or floor vote ever followed, and the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 with the bill still in subcommittee [S1][S5].
The bill drew only one cosponsor among the 256 House Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal operators came out ahead: they avoided a system in which all benefits would be paid from the industry-financed trust fund and in which they would no longer be defendants in black lung cases. Miners and widows with denied or pending claims gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal operators, which avoided expanded liability

for.name: Rep. Nick Rahall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 3, 1993 and delivered introductory remarks; it was his only action as no further stages occurred [S1][S5].

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee / Subcommittee on Labor Standards, Occupational Health and Safety
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 3, 1993 and sent it to the Labor Standards subcommittee on February 19, 1993, then took no further action; no markup, hearing, or vote was ever scheduled [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its single cosponsor were both House Democrats, but no vote was ever taken on the bill, so there is no record of how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill would have ended coal operators' role as defendants with their own counsel in black lung cases and shifted every award onto the industry-financed Black Lung Disability Trust Fund [S2]. The industry's savings from harder-to-win claims were the miners' foregone benefits, so its interest ran against the claimants the bill served.

industries.industry: Coal industry (Black Lung Disability Trust Fund taxpayers)
industries.note: Benefits determined under the new presumptions would all be paid from the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which is financed by the coal industry, increasing the excise-tax burden supporting the fund [S2].
